flashcards.q: Which six hops does a web request pass between the client and the data?
flashcards.a: Client → DNS → CDN → load balancer or gateway → service → datastore. The answer returns along the same road in reverse.
flashcards.more: Think of the pizza place: first learn the address (DNS), take ready-made things from the corner branch (CDN), meet the host at the door (load balancer), then the waiter (your Symfony code) and the oven (the database). A small system may skip the CDN or load balancer, but each hop can break on its own.

flashcards.q: What does DNS do?
flashcards.a: It finds the server's IP address for a domain name such as shop.example.
flashcards.more: A browser can't find a server by name, it needs an IP. DNS is the address book. Answers are cached for a set time (the TTL), so when you change a DNS record it takes a while to reach every user. If DNS breaks, nobody can reach the site even though the servers are healthy.

flashcards.q: What does a CDN do?
flashcards.a: It serves ready-made files such as JS, CSS and images from a server near the user, and forwards everything else to your origin server.
flashcards.more: A CDN has servers in many cities, so files travel a shorter distance and your origin carries less load. There is a risk too: if the CDN caches an old file, users get stale JS. More in [[caching/http-caching/same-file-again|HTTP caching and CDNs]].

flashcards.q: What does a load balancer do?
flashcards.a: It sits in front of several app servers, spreads requests across them and avoids sending any to an unhealthy one.
flashcards.more: It runs health checks to see which servers are responding. If it finds no healthy server it returns a 502 or 503 itself, and if the server behind it takes too long it returns a 504. An API gateway sits in the same place and also handles auth and rate limits.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between 502 Bad Gateway and 504 Gateway Timeout?
flashcards.a: 502: the server behind the proxy refused the connection or sent back a bad answer. 504: it did not answer in time.
flashcards.more: Both are sent by the load balancer or gateway in the middle, not by your app. A 502 usually means the app server is down or restarting. A 504 means the app is up but very slow, often because of a slow database query or an external service.

flashcards.q: Which tells you the request reached your code: 500, or 502/503/504?
flashcards.a: 500. Your own app sends that. 502/503/504 usually come from the load balancer or gateway in front of it.
flashcards.more: With a 500, Symfony's log holds the exception and stack trace, so start there. With a 502/503/504, first check whether the app server is running and what the load balancer's health check says. Knowing who answered cuts the search in half.

flashcards.q: The site is down but the app's log shows no errors. Where do you look?
flashcards.a: At the hops before the app: DNS, CDN, the load balancer. The request never reached the app.
flashcards.more: The app's log only sees requests that reached its code. Test from the outside in: `dig` for DNS, `curl -I` to see who answers, then the load balancer's health check. An empty log does not mean there is no problem.

flashcards.q: When does JavaScript's fetch throw an exception, and when does it not?
flashcards.a: It throws when no response comes back (network, DNS, timeout). It does not throw on a 404 or 500: `res.ok` is just false.
flashcards.more: So catching errors with try/catch alone makes you treat a 500 as a success. Always check `res.ok` or `res.status`, and read the JSON only after that, because a gateway's error page is usually HTML.

flashcards.q: Why does Symfony need trusted_proxies?
flashcards.a: To learn the real client IP and HTTPS behind a load balancer. Otherwise every request seems to come from the load balancer's IP, over HTTP.
flashcards.more: The load balancer writes the real details into the `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto` headers. Symfony believes them only when the sender's IP is on the `trusted_proxies` list. If you trust everyone, anyone can forge a header and pose as a fake IP.

flashcards.q: What is an API contract?
flashcards.a: The agreement between an API and its users: which URL, what to send, and what shape comes back.
flashcards.more: Every field in a response, with its name and type, is part of the contract. As soon as someone depends on it, it becomes a promise, whether or not it is written down. That is why renaming something inside your code is easy, but renaming something in a response is not.

flashcards.q: What is a breaking change?
flashcards.a: A change after which a client that used to work misbehaves or breaks, such as renaming or deleting a field or changing its type.
flashcards.more: The most dangerous break is the one that happens without an error: the server returns 200, but the client's screen shows blank or wrong data. That is why a rename is breaking too, even though it looks small in code.

flashcards.q: What is an additive change, and why is it safe?
flashcards.a: Only adding something new: a new field, a new optional parameter, a new endpoint. Old clients never look at it.
flashcards.more: An old client reads the fields it knows and ignores the rest, so adding doesn't change anything for it. The condition is that a new request parameter must be optional, and its default must keep the old behavior.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between backward and forward compatibility?
flashcards.a: Backward: the new server can still handle old clients. Forward: an older party can cope with fields it doesn't recognize from a newer one.
flashcards.more: Changing an API mainly calls for backward compatibility. Forward compatibility comes from the tolerant reader principle: the client reads only what it needs and doesn't fall apart on unknown fields. With both, server and client can be deployed at different times.

flashcards.q: What is the most common way to version an API, and why?
flashcards.a: A version in the URL path, such as /api/v1/orders. It is simple and visible, and caching and routing stay easy.
flashcards.more: There are header-based and date-based methods too, but they are harder to see and test. For most teams the URL path is the default. If only your own Vue app calls the API and both sides deploy together, you may not need versions at all.

flashcards.q: How do you rename an API field without breaking old clients?
flashcards.a: Send both names for a while, move clients to the new one, measure old usage, and delete the old name only when almost nobody reads it.
flashcards.more: One deploy that renames the field blanks every app that still looks for the old name. Sending both keys is a purely additive change, so it is safe. The price is a slightly bigger response and two keys to keep in step, so fill both from one value.

flashcards.q: How do you run two API versions without writing the logic twice?
flashcards.a: Give each version its own controller and response shape, but call the same application service underneath.
flashcards.more: The business rules live once in the service, so a bug fix helps every version. Only the thin outside layer, the shape of the response, is duplicated. Each extra version still costs tests and docs until it is retired.

flashcards.q: What do the Deprecation and Sunset headers say?
flashcards.a: Deprecation: this API is declared old. Sunset: the exact date it will be shut down.
flashcards.more: If you send both on every old response, client code or monitoring can raise a warning by itself. A `Link` header with `rel="successor-version"` can point to the new version. After the shutdown date you return 410 Gone.

flashcards.q: How is a contract test different from an ordinary test?
flashcards.a: It guards separately what the client expects, so a developer can't hide a break by changing the test along with the code.
flashcards.more: An ordinary test checks the server's current behavior, and when that changes, the test changes with it. A contract test is the client's list of expectations, and changing it means talking to the client. Pact and OpenAPI diff tools are used for this.

flashcards.q: What are over-fetching and under-fetching?
flashcards.a: Over-fetching: getting more data than you need. Under-fetching: not getting enough in one go, so you have to call again and again.
flashcards.more: Both come from REST's fixed-shape resources. On a slow mobile network, both extra data and extra round trips cost a lot. GraphQL was built for exactly these two problems.

flashcards.q: Which style is the usual default, and why?
flashcards.a: REST. Everybody knows it, HTTP caching and tooling are mature, and it is the easiest for outside partners.
flashcards.more: The other styles are cures for specific pains. Bring them in without the pain and you only add the cost of learning, running and debugging them. So start with REST and move when you know where it hurts.

flashcards.q: What problem does GraphQL solve, and what does it cost?
flashcards.a: The client fetches exactly what it wants in one go. The cost: caching is hard, the server is more complex, and heavy queries need limits.
flashcards.more: There is usually a single POST endpoint, so you can't use HTTP caching by URL. Separate database calls for each nested field can cause N+1. Without depth and cost limits, a single query can put pressure on the server.

flashcards.q: Where is gRPC at its best, and where not?
flashcards.a: Between internal services: fast and typed. Not good for browsers or outside partners.
flashcards.more: gRPC uses Protobuf and HTTP/2, so it is compact and fast. But a browser can't speak gRPC directly and needs gRPC-Web or a proxy. It is awkward for outside partners too, because they can't try it with curl.

flashcards.q: Why can't a field number in Protobuf (= 2) be changed?
flashcards.a: On the wire a field is identified by that number, not its name. Change the number and old clients read a different field.
flashcards.more: Renaming a field is relatively safe, but changing or reusing its number is a breaking change. The number of a deleted field is marked `reserved`, so nobody reuses it by mistake.

flashcards.q: What silent failure does gRPC prevent between two internal services?
flashcards.a: A field renamed by the other team. With hand-written JSON you read nothing and carry on; with a generated client the old name stops compiling or fails in CI.
flashcards.more: Both services generate their code from one .proto file, so a change to the contract shows up on both sides before deploy. Hand-written JSON has no such shared file: a missing key is just null, and `?? 0` hides it.

flashcards.q: What does gRPC cost you, and when should you not use it?
flashcards.a: Build tooling (protoc, the gRPC extension) and unreadable binary traffic. Skip it for one team with a few calls, or for clients you don't control.
flashcards.more: A plain REST API described by an OpenAPI file gives most of the contract benefit with none of the tooling. Reach for gRPC when many calls cross services you own, speed matters, or the services use different languages.

flashcards.q: What status does an API return for slow work, and with what?
flashcards.a: `202 Accepted` plus a `Location` header where the job's status can be checked. The work runs in the background in a queue worker.
flashcards.more: 202 honestly says the work was accepted and isn't finished. The client asks that Location now and then to see whether it is pending or done. It is important that a failed job shows as failed, with a reason, in the status, or it stays pending forever.

flashcards.q: What should be the first question when picking a style?
flashcards.a: Where does it hurt, and does it really hurt? If there is no pain, plain REST is right.
flashcards.more: Not "which is modern" but "which problem must I solve". Look at who the clients are, whether the user needs the answer right now, and whether the team can run the style. Mixing styles in one system is fine too: REST outside, gRPC inside.

flashcards.q: Why are OFFSET pages slow?
flashcards.a: The database reads every row up to the OFFSET and throws it away, then returns the rows you asked for. The deeper the page, the higher the cost.
flashcards.more: OFFSET 100000 LIMIT 20 returns 20 rows, but 100,020 have to be read. That is why page 1 is fast and page 5000 is slow. Even with an index, the skipped rows still have to be counted.

flashcards.q: What goes wrong in offset pagination when new rows arrive?
flashcards.a: All the rows shift, so one row shows up on two pages, or a row is skipped.
flashcards.more: If 5 new rows come in at the top after you view page 1, page 2 shows the last 5 rows from before again. When rows are deleted it is the other way around: some rows are never seen. Cursor pagination moves on from the last row you saw, so it doesn't have this problem.

flashcards.q: What is cursor (keyset) pagination in one line?
flashcards.a: Asking for "the next N rows after" the value of the last row you saw, not by page number.
flashcards.more: The query has a `WHERE (created_at, id) < (last value)` condition, and the index goes straight to that spot. So every page is equally fast. The price: "jump to page 50" is not easy.

flashcards.q: When do you choose cursor pagination, and when is offset fine?
flashcards.a: Cursor for big or frequently changing lists (feeds, logs, infinite scroll). Offset for small, stable tables where you need to jump to a page number.
flashcards.more: For an admin panel list of 200 rows, offset is fine, for simplicity. But for lists of millions of rows or a public API, choose cursor, because it handles both deep pages and shifting pages.

flashcards.q: Why does keyset pagination need a tie-breaker?
flashcards.a: If the sort column has equal values, rows get lost. Adding a unique id at the end makes the order completely deterministic.
flashcards.more: `ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC` with the condition `(created_at, id) < (:at, :id)`. With created_at alone, rows from the same second are silently dropped at the page boundary, with no error.

flashcards.q: Why fetch `limit + 1` rows?
flashcards.a: If the extra row arrives, there is a next page. You drop it and build nextCursor, with no separate COUNT.
flashcards.more: COUNT(*) is itself slow on a big table. So cursor APIs usually just report whether there is more: if nextCursor is there, there is; if it is null, you have reached the end.

flashcards.q: Why doesn't the client open up the cursor?
flashcards.a: The cursor is an opaque string. Its internal structure is the server's business, so the client doesn't break when the server changes it.
flashcards.more: The cursor holds created_at and id, but the client only picks up nextCursor each time and sends it back as `after`. A broken cursor should get a 400 from the server. You also have to enforce an upper bound on limit (say 100) on the server.

flashcards.q: Why is it wrong to return 200 OK with "success: false" in the body for a failed job?
flashcards.a: If the status code lies, monitoring, caching and retry tools all make the wrong decision.
flashcards.more: Monitoring usually counts 5xx, so a failure hidden in a 200 shows green on the dashboard. A cache may keep the 200, and the client's ordinary error handling never runs. For a failure, return a real 4xx or 5xx.

flashcards.q: What is the main difference between 4xx and 5xx?
flashcards.a: 4xx means the client's mistake (it has to fix the request and resend). 5xx means the server's mistake (nothing for the client to do).
flashcards.more: Like the courier: with "wrong address" it is no use unless you fix it (4xx), and with "problem at our warehouse" the fault is the courier's (5xx). This split tells you whether a retry can help. With a 4xx, sending again is usually pointless.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between 401 and 403?
flashcards.a: 401: I don't know who you are (not logged in or a bad token). 403: I know who you are, but you have no permission for this.
flashcards.more: With a 401, a new token or logging in may fix it. With a 403, sending again changes nothing, you need permission. When someone tries to open another person's data, many APIs return 404 to hide that it exists.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between 422 and 409?
flashcards.a: 422: the input itself isn't acceptable (a bad email). 409: the input is fine, but it conflicts with the current state (out of stock).
flashcards.more: With a 422, fix it and resend and the job works. With a 409 the client has to look at the new state and decide: ask for fewer, or wait. In both, the body should carry a fixed code.

flashcards.q: What is problem+json?
flashcards.a: A standard JSON shape for describing errors (RFC 9457) with type, title, status and detail; you can add your own code too.
flashcards.more: The Content-Type is `application/problem+json`. If every error goes out in one mould, the client can handle all of them with the same code. Add your own fixed `code`, and the client decides from the code without reading the message.

flashcards.q: Which errors can be retried?
flashcards.a: Temporary ones: 429 (obeying Retry-After), 502/503/504, network errors and timeouts, and even then only for idempotent work.
flashcards.more: 400, 401, 403, 404 and 422 are input or permission mistakes, and sending again gets the same answer. With a 500, if there is a bug, it breaks the same way every time. Before a retry, ask: does doing this job twice do harm?

flashcards.q: How does an idempotency key stop a retry from charging twice?
flashcards.a: The client makes one key per payment and sends it on every retry. The server does the job once per key and replays the saved answer.
flashcards.more: The key lets the server tell a retry from a new payment. It must be made once per user action, not per attempt, and stored where every server can see it. The price is some storage for saved answers, kept for a day or so.

flashcards.q: Which HTTP methods are idempotent?
flashcards.a: GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE and OPTIONS. POST usually isn't, so you make it safe with an idempotency key.
flashcards.more: Idempotent means repeating the same request gives the same result as doing it once. Run DELETE /orders/5 twice and the order is deleted only once. But run POST /payments twice and the money may be charged twice.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between a rate limit and a quota?
flashcards.a: Rate limit: how many requests in a short time (per minute). Quota: the total use over a day or a month.
flashcards.more: A rate limit stops sudden floods and buggy loops. A quota sets the business allowance, such as 100,000 requests a month depending on the plan. Both can return a 429, but they are kept in different places.

flashcards.q: Why do you need a rate limit if nobody is attacking you?
flashcards.a: A buggy loop or bug can fire huge numbers of requests too. One person's mistake must not slow the service for everyone.
flashcards.more: This is called the noisy neighbor problem: one neighbor's racket wears out the whole street. With no limit, the database runs out of connections and ordinary users' pages won't open.

flashcards.q: How does a token bucket work?
flashcards.a: Tokens collect in a bucket over time. Each request spends one. When the bucket is empty, you have to wait.
flashcards.more: There are two numbers: the size of the bucket (how big a burst) and the refill rate (the average). Short bursts are tolerated, but under sustained pressure the average rate rules. In Symfony RateLimiter, `limit` is the size and `rate` is the rate.

flashcards.q: What is the weakness of a fixed window?
flashcards.a: Twice the limit can get in at the window boundary: 100 at the end of one minute and 100 at the start of the next.
flashcards.more: That is because the count resets to zero when the window ends. A sliding window counts over any running 60 seconds, so there is no such gap. But it needs more memory.

flashcards.q: What status and header does an API send when the limit is exceeded?
flashcards.a: `429 Too Many Requests` and a `Retry-After` header saying how many seconds to wait before trying again.
flashcards.more: In Symfony, throwing `TooManyRequestsHttpException($retryAfterSeconds)` produces both. The client reads Retry-After and returns at the right time. If it is missing, the client backs off by itself.

flashcards.q: Why must a rate-limit key be something a client can't invent for free?
flashcards.a: If the key is an unchecked header, a client sends a new random value on every request and gets a fresh bucket each time. Use a verified key, the user id or the IP.
flashcards.more: Each distinct key gets its own bucket, so a limit only holds if a client can't mint keys at will. Look the API key up in your database first; if it isn't known, fall back to the IP. The same thinking applies to any value the client controls.

flashcards.q: Why use exponential backoff and jitter together?
flashcards.a: Backoff doubles the wait each time. Jitter makes it random, so a thousand clients don't return at the same instant.
flashcards.more: Without jitter every client comes back in step after 1, 2, 4 seconds, and the server goes down again. Random waits spread them over time. Retry only idempotent requests.

flashcards.q: What goes wrong if you rate limit by IP alone?
flashcards.a: Many people share one IP (mobile carriers, offices), so one person's fault blocks everyone. Behind a load balancer, everyone's IP can look the same.
flashcards.more: Use the user id for logged-in users, and the API key for outside clients. Keep the IP for unknown traffic before login. With a load balancer, unless `trusted_proxies` is right, you won't get the real IP.

flashcards.q: What does thin client mean?
flashcards.a: A client that makes no business decisions itself; it only shows what the server gives it and sends the user's input.
flashcards.more: Rules like price, discount, permissions and stock are written once on the server. Web, mobile and partners all get the same answer. The client's job is to display things and be convenient.

flashcards.q: What are the three problems with keeping business rules in the client?
flashcards.a: A separate (possibly wrong) copy in each client, a release everywhere to change a rule, and users can alter the calculation themselves.
flashcards.more: A mobile app can be stuck in app store review, and old versions run for months. A partner's site doesn't have your rules at all. And browser DevTools can change any value being sent.

flashcards.q: Why can't you trust the `total` the client sends?
flashcards.a: A user can change any value using DevTools or by calling the API directly. The price has to come from the server's own calculation.
flashcards.more: The right design: the client sends only the product id and quantity. The server takes the real prices from the database, works out the subtotal, discount and total, and returns them. The client just displays them.

flashcards.q: A client sends {"items": [...], "total": 1}. Why is the stored total still correct?
flashcards.a: The request class declares only items, so total is never read. The order is built from a Quote that the server calculates from database prices.
flashcards.more: This is the whole fix in one line: no field the client controls ever reaches the price. If the client needs a live total while the user edits the cart, give it a quote endpoint that calls the same PriceCalculator, and build the real order from a fresh quote.

flashcards.q: Which checks are fine in the client, and which aren't?
flashcards.a: Fine: up-front checks for the user's convenience (does the email contain @). Wrong: having the client as the only check.
flashcards.more: Client checks give quick feedback, but can be skipped at any time. The real validation and rules are always on the server. Having both is good, having only the client is dangerous.

flashcards.q: How does the client know which button to show if the rules are on the server?
flashcards.a: The response carries `abilities`-style flags, such as `cancel: true`. The client shows or hides the button from them.
flashcards.more: The server runs the Voter and reports the result, and the client never learns the rule. Even so, the real action's endpoint must check again with #[IsGranted], because hiding a button is not security.

flashcards.q: What is a BFF (Backend for Frontend)?
flashcards.a: Backend for Frontend: a thin server per client that joins and trims the core services' data to fit that client's screen.
flashcards.more: Its job is to merge, say, three API calls into one response for mobile. But price and permission rules don't go here, they stay in the core service. Otherwise the rules get duplicated across the BFFs.

flashcards.q: When is a BFF not needed?
flashcards.a: When there is only one client, or web and mobile need almost the same thing. Then the extra server is just a burden.
flashcards.more: A BFF brings the cost of running and deploying an extra service. You only get the benefit when the screens really differ and different teams build them. GraphQL solves a similar problem too.
